biographical-essays: Thomas De Quincey, famous for his Confessions of an English Opium-Eater, turns his restless mind to the lives of others in these essays. Poets, thinkers, and public figures of his age come under his close and often surprising gaze. De Quincey's prose runs rich and winding, full of asides and sudden insights, making these portraits as much about his own way of seeing as about the men he describes.
lectures-and-essays: Thomas Henry Huxley — Darwin's bulldog — was Victorian England's fiercest champion of science, and these lectures and essays show why. He writes on evolution, education, and the place of science in modern life with unmatched clarity and fighting spirit. Readers meet one of the great popularizers of science, making difficult ideas thrilling to a general audience.
king-arthur-s-socks-and-other-village-pl: Writer and activist Floyd Dell offers a set of short, witty one-act plays designed for amateur village theaters. The title play gently spoofs small-town pretensions with affection rather than cruelty. Practical, funny, and easy to stage, the collection gave community players ready-made entertainment with a literary touch.
hello-boys: Ella Wheeler Wilcox addresses the soldiers of the Great War in these rousing verses of encouragement and cheer. Written to lift the spirits of boys far from home, the poems celebrate courage, comradeship, and the folks back home. A heartfelt example of how poetry served on the home front.
old-caravan-days: Mary Hartwell Catherwood's pioneer tale follows the old caravan days — wagon trains, frontier forts, and the slow westward march of settlement. Her sympathetic portraits of settlers and Native peoples alike set her apart. A warm, well-crafted story of the American migration.
science-education-essays: Thomas Henry Huxley, Darwin's bulldog, argues for science in education in these powerful essays. His clear, fighting prose made the case that won the schools. The charter of modern scientific teaching. Laboratories for schoolboys was his cry, and the world at last has heard it.
tropic-days: E. J. Banfield's Tropic Days continues his Dunk Island chronicles — more birds, reefs, and island lore from the Great Barrier Reef. His gentle observations never pall. A worthy sequel to My Tropic Isle. Reef herons, beach stone-curlews, and island nights fill his pages.
castilian-days: John Hay, Lincoln's secretary and a great statesman, sketches Castilian days — Spain in the 1870s, vivid and observant. His keen American eye catches the country's color, pride, and character. Delightful travel writing from a man of affairs who loved the old world.
